book.title: Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies
book.author: Jim Collins; Jerry I. Porras

edition.name: Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies
edition.sourceProvenance: Authorized preview bundle centered on Google Books, cross-checked with Open Library and official Jim Collins materials.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Money tells you whether a company can keep going. It does not fully tell you what the company is for. That is the pressure inside More Than Profits. A business needs profit, but profit alone is too thin to hold an institution together across changing leaders and changing conditions.

The chapter says durable companies need a deeper center made of values and purpose. That deeper center gives people a reason to protect certain choices even when easy money points somewhere else. It also gives the company something stable that can survive leadership turnover.

So the test is simple. When pressure rises, does the company have values that shape the decision, or does profit settle everything by itself? If profit settles everything, the stated purpose is decoration.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The chapter does not dismiss profit. It changes profit's rank. Profit is necessary for survival, but it is not the deepest organizing center of a durable company.

Collins's official language about core values and purpose gives the chapter its spine. A strong organization has an enduring character that outlasts particular leaders. That character comes from what the institution believes and what it exists to serve, not just from the quarter's numbers.

That is why the chapter cares about real constraint. Values matter only when they shape decisions under pressure. If they never cost anything, they are not functioning as a core.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Profit is easy to count, which is why people are tempted to let it explain everything. The chapter says that is too cheap. Profit can keep the lights on and still fail to tell a company what deserves protection when the fast money pushes in the wrong direction.

A durable company needs a center deeper than the scoreboard. Core values and purpose give the institution a character that can survive leadership change and still guide choices.

The hard test comes under pressure. If the company's values disappear the moment money gets loud, then the values were branding language, not a core.

point.direct: Profit is necessary without being the highest center.
point.competitive: The scoreboard is too thin to be the soul of the company.

oneMinuteRecap.competitive: If money settles every argument, the so-called values are stage props.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Money is the cleanest part of a company story. You can count it, compare it, and track it over time. That clarity is useful, but it can tempt people into treating profit as the whole reason a company exists. The chapter says that is too thin. Profit can tell you whether a business is viable. It cannot fully tell you what deserves protection when leadership changes or pressure rises.

That is why More Than Profits puts profit in a different place rather than throwing it away. A company still has to earn enough to survive and keep going. But survival conditions are not the same thing as institutional purpose. Collins's official writing about core values and purpose gives the chapter its backbone. A strong organization has an enduring character that goes beyond any given set of people.

That enduring character matters because no institution can stay itself if every leadership transition resets the reason for being there. A company held together only by financial incentive may perform for a while, but it has no stable answer to what must remain constant when conditions shift. Core values and purpose solve that differently. They give the company a center that survives founder turnover, executive turnover, and market pressure.

The chapter becomes more demanding when it turns toward real decisions. Almost any organization can draft noble words. The issue is whether those words constrain action when gain points somewhere else. If profit is always the final answer, then the values are decorative. The chapter is not asking for prettier mission language. It is asking for a core that can tell the company what not to trade away.

That is the hard usefulness of the chapter. It gives durability direction. A clock-building company still needs to know what it is preserving. Profit matters, but it is not enough to provide identity by itself. The institution needs a purpose and a set of values that can outlast leaders and shape choices when the easy path is available.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The chapter begins with a ranking problem. Profit is essential to survival, but it is too thin to serve as the deepest organizing center of a durable company. Collins and Porras are not arguing that money does not matter. They are arguing that money alone cannot provide enduring character.

That distinction matters because institutions have to survive leadership turnover. Collins's official framing around core values and purpose says the enduring character of a strong organization lives beyond any given set of people. If the company's center changes every time the leadership team changes, then the company does not really have a center at all. It has a rotating set of preferences attached to whoever currently holds power.

The chapter therefore treats purpose and values as structural, not decorative. They tell the organization what deserves continuity when tactics, markets, and leaders change. Profit supports continuation, but core ideology shapes what continuation is for. Without that deeper layer, the company may still function, but it becomes more vulnerable to drift because it lacks a stable answer to what should remain non-negotiable.

This is where the chapter becomes stricter than typical purpose talk. Values only count when they constrain action under pressure. If they disappear the moment a profitable shortcut appears, then they were not functioning as values in the first place. The chapter forces a hard diagnostic question: what decision would this value actually change?

That question protects the chapter from sentimentality. A real core is not website language or leadership theater. It is the part of the institution that survives leadership change and still shapes costly decisions. Profit matters, but the company needs something deeper if it wants durability to mean more than continued revenue generation.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Profit is the easiest thing in a company to measure, which is exactly why people are tempted to let it explain the whole institution. The chapter says that move is lazy. Profit can tell you whether the business is alive. It cannot fully tell you what the business stands for when gain and identity start pulling in different directions.

That is why Collins's language about core values and purpose matters so much here. A durable company needs an enduring character that does not vanish when the current leaders do. If the center rotates with every new executive voice, then the company is not really preserving anything. It is just staying financially active while drifting from one power center to the next.

The chapter is not anti-profit. It is anti-thinness. Profit is necessary, but it is too weak to act as the deepest answer to what the institution is for. Core ideology gives the company a reason to protect certain choices even when those choices are not the easiest route to immediate gain.

This is where vague purpose talk gets exposed. Noble language is cheap. Constraint is expensive. If a stated value never changes a hard decision, then it is not doing any real work inside the organization. It is decoration for people who want the prestige of principles without the discipline of them.

So the chapter's demand is sharp. Show the core where it hurts. Show it in the choices that cost something. If the company cannot do that, then money is still the only real center, no matter how polished the values statement sounds.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Money gives leaders a seductive kind of clarity. It is countable, comparable, and easy to use as the final answer in an argument. Companies drift toward acting as if profit explains their entire reason for being for exactly that reason. Chapter 3 resists the drift. Profit can tell you whether the business can continue. It cannot fully tell you what should remain constant when power changes hands or pressure starts pushing against the company's character.

More Than Profits is not an anti-business chapter. It is a hierarchy chapter. Profit belongs in the survival layer. Core values and purpose belong in the identity layer. Collins's official writing on enduring character matters here because it places the center of the institution beyond any given set of leaders. The company needs a reason to remain itself that does not vanish when the current leadership team does.

This distinction matters most when leadership turns over. A company held together only by financial incentive may still perform, but it has no durable answer to what must not be traded away. Without core values and purpose, continuity becomes thin. The institution may continue operating while drifting from one power preference to the next. Hard depth has to keep that risk visible because drift can happen inside a profitable company just as easily as inside a weak one.

That is where the chapter's real analytical edge appears. It does not treat values as warm language. It treats them as a mechanism of constraint. If profit is the only thing that ever settles the hard decision, then the values are not functioning as a core. They are functioning as decoration. A real core changes what the organization will and will not do, even when the easier money points the other way.

This creates a useful tension the chapter cannot dodge. Purpose language is cheap. Almost any company can produce statements about service, meaning, or belief. The chapter becomes convincing only when those statements survive contact with sacrifice. What does the company refuse? What kind of gain does it reject? What continuity does it protect when the short run offers a tempting shortcut? Those questions separate enduring character from polished theater.

There is also a boundary condition here. Purpose can become vague, manipulative, or self-flattering if leaders use it without operational consequence. Calling ordinary preference a sacred value is one of the easiest ways to make the chapter sentimental and false. Hard depth has to keep that danger visible. A real ideology should help the institution distinguish between what is genuinely core and what is merely comfortable or familiar.

That leaves the central threshold alive. What proves that a company's values are a real core rather than a flattering script wrapped around ordinary profit-seeking? The chapter's answer is demanding: the core must outlast leaders, shape costly decisions, and give continuity a direction deeper than financial success alone. Once that core exists, the next challenge becomes just as difficult. How do you preserve it without confusing preservation with rigidity?
chapterBreakdown.direct:
A durable company can keep operating and still fail to know what it is preserving. That is the difference between viability and identity. Profit determines whether a company can continue operating. It does not fully determine what the company is for or what should remain stable when conditions change. Durable institutions therefore need a center deeper than the financial scoreboard.

Collins's official language about core values and purpose gives the chapter its strongest support. An enduring character belongs to the organization beyond any given set of people. That means the institution cannot rely on current leaders alone to define its meaning. If the center rotates whenever the leadership roster rotates, then the company has continuity of operation without continuity of character.

That distinction becomes more important, not less, when a company is profitable. Profit can hide drift because it makes leaders feel justified. The organization may still be earning while quietly losing any stable answer to what it exists to preserve. Hard depth has to surface that possibility. A financially successful company can still become ideologically thin if it has no deeper layer than revenue generation.

This is why the chapter treats values and purpose as structural constraints rather than as emotional language. A real value changes what the company is willing to do under pressure. If profit settles every serious argument, then values are not governing. They are decorative. The chapter's strongest diagnostic question is therefore practical rather than poetic: what decision would this value actually change?

That question also reveals the chapter's main failure mode. Leaders can use purpose language manipulatively. They can elevate convenient habits into sacred principles or deploy noble words that never face costly tradeoffs. Without a visible decision consequence, the claim of core ideology remains weak. Hard depth has to preserve that skepticism so the chapter does not collapse into mission-statement theater.

The chapter therefore lands on a rigorous definition of deeper center. Profit matters because viability matters. But identity, continuity, and character require something more. A durable company needs values and purpose that outlast leaders, govern costly choices, and keep the institution from drifting into whatever the short run currently rewards. The next chapter has to answer the obvious tension that follows: how can such a core remain stable without becoming a pretext for stagnation?
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Profit is seductive because it ends arguments fast. It is measurable, defensible, and easy to treat as the only adult voice in the room. Chapter 3 says that habit makes companies thinner than they realize. Profit can keep the institution alive while still failing to tell it what deserves loyalty when gain and character collide.

The chapter pushes toward core values and purpose for exactly that reason. Collins's official framing is useful because it places enduring character beyond any particular set of leaders. If the center of the company changes every time power changes hands, then the company is not preserving anything deeper than temporary preference. It is just staying in business while drifting.

This is where profitable companies can fool themselves most easily. Strong numbers create a false sense that the institution must be coherent because the institution is succeeding. Not true. Revenue can mask ideological weakness for a long time. A company can keep earning while quietly losing any stable answer to what it will not trade away.

That is why the chapter treats values as constraint rather than decoration. A value becomes real when it blocks an attractive move, redirects a tempting shortcut, or forces the company to absorb a cost it would rather avoid. If money wins every serious argument, then the values statement is set dressing for profit-seeking with better typography.

The danger runs both ways. Some leaders use purpose talk honestly. Others use it to crown familiar preferences with moral prestige. That is the chapter's hard limit. A fake core can be just as dangerous as no core because it teaches the organization to protect comfort while pretending to protect principle.

So the chapter's demand is severe and useful. Show the core in the choices that cost something. Show it surviving leadership turnover. Show it telling the institution what not to become even when the short run pays well. Otherwise profit is still the only real center, and the noble language is just camouflage. The next question then becomes unavoidable: if the company finally has a real core, how does it keep that core alive without turning it into a museum piece?

examples.title: Tessa Tests Whether the Value Statement Can Beat the Pricing Memo

scenario.gentle: Tessa sits at a conference table with a pricing memo that would boost margins quickly by hiding a service limitation in the fine print. Her company says it values trust and long-term relationships. She has to decide whether those words are real enough to change the decision in front of her.
scenario.direct: A pricing proposal on Tessa's table would increase revenue by making one weak service term harder for customers to notice. The company speaks often about trust. Tessa now has the chapter's real question in her hands: does that stated value actually constrain the profitable move?
scenario.competitive: The margin lift is obvious. So is the test. Tessa can protect the quarter or force the company to prove that trust is more than typography on the wall.

whatToDo.gentle: Reject the hidden-term shortcut and ask for a version that keeps the offer transparent even if the margin gain shrinks.
whatToDo.direct: Treat trust as a governing value and rewrite the proposal so the customer sees the limitation clearly.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the value beat the easy money once. Otherwise stop pretending it is a core.

whyItMatters.gentle: A company's values become believable when they change an attractive decision, not when they sound good in a meeting.
whyItMatters.direct: This is the chapter's central test: does the value constrain a profitable shortcut or disappear in front of it?
whyItMatters.competitive: If the pricing memo wins untouched, the value statement just got exposed.

examples.title: Arun Asks Whether the Club Mission Still Governs Choices

scenario.gentle: Arun sits in a room lined with old service-club banners while officers debate dropping their tutoring program because a louder fundraising event would attract more applause. The club says its purpose is helping local students directly. Arun wants to know whether that purpose is real or ceremonial.
scenario.direct: The officers want to replace the club's tutoring program with a flashier event that would raise more money and bring more campus attention. Arun hears the argument and realizes the chapter's question applies perfectly: is the mission a real guide, or only something printed on the banner?
scenario.competitive: The banner says one thing. The room wants another. Arun has to force the club to decide whether its mission can beat an easier path to attention.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask, "If direct student support is our mission, what decision should that mission change right here?"
whatToDo.direct: Push the officers to show how the mission constrains the choice instead of treating it as decorative language.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the mission earn its space on the wall by making it win a real argument.

whyItMatters.gentle: A group's purpose only becomes durable when it survives a tempting alternative.
whyItMatters.direct: The mission is real only if it guides action under pressure.
whyItMatters.competitive: If applause beats purpose every time, the purpose is fake.

examples.title: Maya Wonders Why the Family Store Stays Open

scenario.gentle: Maya counts the cash drawer at closing and hears her uncle say, "If this store ever stops being profitable, none of this means anything anyway." She knows the family also talks about serving the neighborhood and keeping a certain standard of honesty. She is trying to decide whether those values are real or just comforting language around the numbers.
scenario.direct: At closing time, Maya hears the store's future reduced to one line: if the money works, the business is worth keeping; if it doesn't, nothing else matters. She knows the family claims a deeper purpose than that. The chapter's pressure lands hard here: what, if anything, would they protect even when profit pushes the other way?
scenario.competitive: The cash drawer is real. So is the excuse it can become. Maya can feel the family sliding toward a world where money settles every argument and the rest of the values talk becomes theater.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask the family to name one practice they would refuse to abandon even if a shortcut would increase profit.
whatToDo.direct: Turn the conversation from sentiment into proof by asking which value would actually constrain an attractive move.
whatToDo.competitive: Force the family to show one place where the core can beat the cash drawer.

whyItMatters.gentle: A family business can honor profit without letting profit erase the reason the business exists.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter's test is whether there is a real center deeper than survival accounting.
whyItMatters.competitive: If money always gets final veto, the so-called purpose is camouflage.

examples.title: Joel Tests the Purpose Statement at the Strategy Offsite

scenario.gentle: Joel reads the offsite packet and notices the company's purpose statement sits on the first page while the proposed strategy on page seven would likely violate it for faster growth. He wants to know whether the statement is a real operating center or just respectful decoration.
scenario.direct: At an executive offsite, Joel sees a polished purpose statement on the opening slide and a growth move later in the packet that clearly conflicts with it. He needs to decide whether to call out the contradiction or let the statement keep functioning as ceremonial language.
scenario.competitive: The packet is trying to have it both ways: noble purpose on page one, opportunism on page seven. Joel can either let the room enjoy both or make them choose which one actually governs the company.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask, "If we approve this move, what exactly does our stated purpose still rule?"
whatToDo.direct: Use the proposed contradiction to test whether the purpose statement constrains strategy or merely accompanies it.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the room decide whether purpose is a governor or wallpaper.

whyItMatters.gentle: A purpose statement becomes credible only when it survives contact with a tempting strategic shortcut.

examples.title: Naomi Asks What Would Survive the Officer Election

scenario.gentle: Naomi sits in the student government office after elections, looking at old posters and notes from different officer teams. She wonders what, if anything, has stayed the same across those handoffs besides the budget. That question becomes her way of testing whether the group has a real core.
scenario.direct: Leadership just turned over again, and Naomi is reviewing what the student government actually preserves from year to year. If the answer is only access to funds and room bookings, the institution may be operating without a deeper center.
scenario.competitive: Every election produces a fresh personality. Naomi wants to know whether anything deeper than convenience survives the turnover.

whatToDo.gentle: Write down the principles or commitments that should remain recognizable no matter which students hold office next.
whatToDo.direct: Test the institution by asking what should survive leadership change besides operational control.
whatToDo.competitive: Strip away the personalities and see whether the group still has a center.

whyItMatters.gentle: A real core should remain legible even when the leaders rotate.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter links durability to what survives beyond current officeholders.
whyItMatters.competitive: If turnover erases the center, there never was one.

examples.title: Felix Calls Out the Family's Favorite Slogan

scenario.gentle: Felix's siblings keep saying, "Family first," but he notices the phrase never changes any real decision when money or convenience push the other way. During an argument about selling part of the family business, he feels the chapter's question pressing in: is the slogan a value or just something they like hearing?
scenario.direct: In a family argument over the business, everyone repeats the same moral slogan, yet none of them can point to a tradeoff the slogan has ever actually governed. Felix wants to challenge the language without sounding cynical.
scenario.competitive: The family loves a slogan that has never had to bleed. Felix can feel how little it governs and how much comfort it provides. He has to decide whether to puncture that comfort.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask, "What decision has that principle actually changed for us when it cost something?"
whatToDo.direct: Turn the slogan into a decision test and ask for the concrete tradeoff it has governed.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the slogan pay rent. If it cannot survive a costly example, stop calling it core.

Reject the hidden-term shortcut and force the company to honor the value in the proposal

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether a value can actually change a profitable decision when pressure is real.
explanation.direct: Treating trust as core means letting it constrain the proposal rather than decorating it.
explanation.competitive: The value has to beat the easy money at least once or it was never governing.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the strongest trap answer for this chapter?
choices: Since profit is not the deepest center, financial discipline does not matter much
A durable company needs both viability and a deeper core beyond viability
Purpose becomes credible only when it shapes real tradeoffs

explanation.gentle: The chapter never dismisses profit. It changes profit's rank, not its necessity.
explanation.direct: Option A mistakes a hierarchy argument for an anti-business argument.
explanation.competitive: The chapter is not giving anyone permission to romanticize weakness.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main warning about purpose language?
choices: Purpose language should be avoided because it is always manipulative
Purpose language can become fake if leaders use it without operational consequence
Purpose language matters only in nonprofit settings

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps a real skepticism alive: purpose talk becomes weak if it never changes costly choices.
explanation.direct: Its failure mode is decorative ideology, not ideology itself.
explanation.competitive: Noble language without sacrifice is camouflage.

questions.prompt: A student club says its mission is direct service, but it keeps choosing flashy events that bring more attention instead. What question best applies the chapter?
choices: What mission statement sounds better to new members?
What decision is the mission actually changing right now?
How can the club avoid all fundraising from now on?

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether the mission can guide a real choice under pressure.
explanation.direct: The strongest test is decision consequence, not language quality.
explanation.competitive: If the mission cannot win one argument, it is just banner text.

questions.prompt: Joel sees a strategy packet where the purpose statement on page one conflicts with the growth move on page seven. What is the strongest response?
choices: Ignore the contradiction because growth strategy should always outrank purpose
Ask what the purpose statement still governs if the company approves the move anyway
Remove the purpose statement from future packets to avoid hypocrisy

explanation.gentle: The chapter turns purpose into a test of what the company will protect under pressure.
explanation.direct: Joel should use the contradiction to see whether the purpose statement functions as a real governor or only as ceremony.
explanation.competitive: Make the room choose between a real core and expensive wallpaper.

questions.prompt: What best shows that a company's deeper center is real rather than leader-dependent?
choices: The values remain visible and decision-relevant even after leadership turnover
The founder continues giving strong speeches after retirement
The company earns enough money to keep operating

explanation.gentle: The chapter looks for what survives beyond current leaders while still guiding choices.
explanation.direct: A deeper center is institutional when it outlasts leader turnover and continues shaping costly decisions.
explanation.competitive: If the core still rules after the personalities rotate, then the core is finally real.

questions.prompt: If a company has a real core deeper than profit, what tension naturally comes next in the book's logic?
choices: How to preserve that core without freezing the company's methods
How to eliminate all pressure from future decisions
How to make values identical across every industry

explanation.gentle: The next step asks how an institution can protect its core while still moving and adapting.
explanation.direct: The bridge forward is the tension between preserving identity and stimulating progress.
explanation.competitive: Once the company gets a center, the next risk is turning that center into dead weight.

coreSkill.gentle: The core skill is learning to tell the difference between a company's survival engine and its deeper center.
coreSkill.direct: The chapter teaches purpose hierarchy and constraint diagnosis.
coreSkill.competitive: The skill is exposing when profit is still the only real ruler in the room.

plan.gentle: If a company value is mentioned in a meeting, then ask what decision that value would actually change under pressure.
plan.direct: If leaders invoke purpose, then test it against a profitable shortcut and see whether it governs anything concrete.
plan.competitive: If the value sounds noble, then force it into a costly tradeoff before you trust it.

plan.gentle: If a club repeats its mission often, then name one decision the mission should control this semester.
plan.direct: If a school group claims a purpose, then test whether that purpose constrains an attractive alternative.
plan.competitive: If the mission cannot beat applause once, stop pretending it is the center.

plan.gentle: If your family says a principle matters, then ask for one example where that principle would cost something real.
plan.direct: If a family or small business claims a core value, then check whether the value changes what is acceptable when money pushes the other way.
plan.competitive: If the principle never loses comfort or cash, it is still just a slogan.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: In the next day, take one stated value from an organization you know and write the hard decision that would prove it is real.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Within 24 hours, test one purpose claim by naming the profitable move it should be able to block.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Next day: pick one polished value and make it face a tradeoff it cannot dodge.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, notice one place where money settles an argument and ask whether a deeper core ever gets a vote there.
weeklyPractice.direct: Do one weekly audit of a claimed value and judge it by whether it constrained action under pressure.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Every week, catch one point where profit is still the only real sovereign despite the noble language.

front.gentle: What is profit too thin to do by itself in this chapter?
front.direct: What deeper job can profit not fully perform?
front.competitive: What can the scoreboard not define on its own?

back.gentle: Profit cannot fully define the institution's deeper purpose or what should remain constant over time.
back.direct: Profit can support viability without providing enduring character by itself.
back.competitive: The scoreboard can keep the company alive and still fail to tell it who it is.

front.gentle: Why does the chapter care about values surviving leader turnover?
front.direct: What does leadership change test here?
front.competitive: What gets exposed when the boss changes?

back.gentle: Leader turnover tests whether the company's center belongs to the institution or only to current personalities.
back.direct: A real core should remain meaningful beyond any particular set of leaders.
back.competitive: If the center rotates with the boss, it was never a center.

front.gentle: When do values become real instead of decorative?
front.direct: What is the chapter's test for a true value?
front.competitive: What turns a value from wallpaper into rule?

back.gentle: Values become real when they shape a hard decision under pressure.
back.direct: Constraint is the test: a real value changes what the company is willing to do.
back.competitive: A value becomes rule when it can beat an attractive shortcut.

front.gentle: How can strong profits still hide weakness according to this chapter?
front.direct: What kind of drift can profitability mask?
front.competitive: How can success camouflage a thin center?

back.gentle: A company can earn well while quietly losing clarity about what it exists to preserve.
back.direct: Profitability can mask ideological drift by making the institution feel justified despite weak core guidance.
back.competitive: Good numbers can make hollow institutions look coherent for longer than they deserve.

front.gentle: What is the chapter's main warning about purpose talk?
front.direct: How can purpose language fail while still sounding impressive?
front.competitive: What does camouflage ideology look like?

back.gentle: Purpose language fails when it sounds noble but never changes costly choices.
back.direct: A fake core imitates principle in language while avoiding operational consequence.
back.competitive: Camouflage ideology is polished language protecting comfort or gain.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: A durable company needs more than financial success. It needs values and purpose that survive leader turnover and change real decisions when pressure rises.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Profit keeps the institution viable, but core values and purpose give the institution enduring character and real constraint.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: If money wins every serious argument, the company still has one real center and the noble language is camouflage.
